findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the loser's behavior on lock contention: wait for the winner to release, then re-run the verify-HEAD check (observing the completed clone) rather than skipping provisioning and exec'ing over an unresolvable store.
evidence: Provisioning runs backgrounded then 'exec "$@"' (Dockerfile.mcp:114-115), so once provision_store returns the server is already serving.

The AC states the loser 'observes the winner's completed clone' but the plan gives no mechanism for the loser to BLOCK until the winner completes and then re-check HEAD; if the loser just skips on lock-contention it exits provision_store while the store is still unresolvable.
The read guard (store_uninitialized) will report loudly, but no later container re-clones — the failure mode this ticket names ('No later container re-clones').
findings.finding: The 'loser observes the winner's completed clone' acceptance criterion does not specify how the loser waits for and re-evaluates the store after the winner finishes; a loser that merely fails to acquire the lock and falls through to `exec` serves an empty store with nothing left to re-provision it.
findings.location: Additional acceptance criteria: 'the loser observes the winner's completed clone instead of re-cloning'
scenarios: Two containers race; the loser skips provisioning and its server serves store_uninitialized indefinitely until an unrelated restart

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Justify why a hand-rolled hard-linked-timestamp lock is used instead of the flock the codebase already standardizes on (autodeploy.sh `flock -n 9`; rebar `fcntl.flock`+mkdir), given the mcp container is Linux and flock auto-releases on holder death — making AC5 free and AC4's race/wedge modes moot; adopt flock unless a specific disqualifier is documented.
evidence: Plan: 'the re-clone takes a lock. Acquisition must be atomic WITH its timestamp (a hard-linked file written before it is linked into place)'
Plan AC5: 'A container that dies holding the lock does not wedge the store permanently.' — this is flock's built-in behavior, not something to hand-build
autodeploy.sh:436-437 `exec 9>"$LOCK"; flock -n 9 || { log "another deploy holds the lock; skipping"; exit 0; }` — same 'serialize concurrent runs' shape
README.md:140-143 documents rebar's own `fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX)` + `mkdir` fallback as the sanctioned cross-process lock with no external-tool dependency
Dockerfile.mcp:16 `FROM python:3.12-slim` (Linux) — flock(1) and fcntl.flock both available in-container
findings.finding: Scope-growth #2 designs a hand-rolled cross-container lock (hard-linked file + embedded atomic acquired-at timestamp + stale-detection + stale-breaking + death-recovery) that rebuilds a locking primitive the codebase already standardizes on. autodeploy.sh serializes overlapping runs with `flock -n 9` on a lockfile (autodeploy.sh:436-437) for the identical purpose, and rebar's store uses `fcntl.flock` + atomic-`mkdir` fallback (src/rebar/_store/lock.py, _snapshot/cache.py, alert_store.py, reducer/marker.py). flock is kernel-released on holder death, so AC5 ('a container that dies holding the lock does not wedge the store') is inherent to flock but must be hand-built as a timestamp reaper under the proposed scheme; and AC4's own stated failure modes ('a lock that exists briefly without a readable marker is either a race ... or a permanent wedge') are exactly the races flock's atomic acquisition avoids. The mcp image is Debian-based Linux (Dockerfile.mcp FROM python:3.12-slim) where both flock(1) and fcntl.flock are available.
findings.location: Scope growth #2 ('Serialize the re-clone across containers'), and Additional acceptance criteria bullets 3-5
scenarios: Two containers with overlapping provisioning windows both try to acquire the clone lock
A container is SIGKILLed mid-clone while holding the lock
findings.suggested_fix: Serialize the re-clone with `flock` on a lockfile in the volume (mirroring autodeploy.sh:436-437: `exec 9>"$DIR/.provision.lock"; flock 9`), taken around the verify->clear->clone critical section, with the loser re-checking HEAD after acquiring. flock's kernel auto-release on process death satisfies AC5 with no timestamp reaper, and its atomic acquisition removes the race/wedge window AC4 is written to defend against.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the stale-lock threshold (or a liveness/heartbeat signal) so it exceeds the maximum legitimate ~200k-commit clone duration, so a slow-but-healthy clone is never declared stale while a truly dead holder is still eventually reclaimed.
evidence: Provisioning is backgrounded precisely because 'the ~200k-commit clone outruns the 120s readiness deadline' (section 2).
The plan requires stale-lock breaking ('peers read it as stale and break it') and atomic timestamping, but states no staleness threshold and does not tie it to the maximum clone time.
If the stale threshold is shorter than a legitimate clone, the winner's lock is broken mid-clone and a peer clear-and-clones over it — the exact concurrent-poisoning mechanism section 2 describes.
findings.finding: The stale-lock threshold is not specified relative to the maximum legitimate clone duration, so a slow-but-healthy clone can have its lock broken by a peer — reintroducing the poisoning this ticket removes.
findings.location: Scope growth section 2 + AC 'A container that dies holding the lock does not wedge the store permanently.'
scenarios: A cold clone of the ~200k-commit branch taking many minutes on a slow network
A peer container starting while the first is still legitimately cloning

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Evaluate clone-to-temp-then-atomic-rename as an alternative to in-place clear-and-clone: publishing the fresh clone via rename is atomic, so a peer never observes a half-cleared dir and much of the section-2 lock/stale-detection machinery becomes unnecessary; state why the chosen in-place approach is preferred if it is retained.
evidence: Chosen mechanism: 'rm -rf "$DIR"/.[!.]* "$DIR"/*; git clone ... "$DIR"' clears IN PLACE, so a peer mid-clone can be cleared out from under (the plan's own section-2 poisoning mechanism).

An alternative — clone into $DIR.tmp then `mv`/rename into $DIR — makes the publish atomic: a peer only ever sees the old store or the fully-cloned new one, never a half-cleared dir, which removes most of the need for the flock + atomic-timestamp + stale-break machinery in section 2.
ABSENCE: the plan states no positive reason for preferring in-place clear over atomic-rename despite adopting the more complex lock design to compensate for in-place's hazard.
findings.finding: The plan does not consider clone-to-a-temp-dir-then-atomic-rename, which is structurally simpler and more robust than the chosen in-place clear-and-clone-under-a-lock for the concurrency hazard the plan itself identifies.
findings.location: Fix section + Scope growth section 2 (Serialize the re-clone)
scenarios: Two containers whose provisioning windows overlap on the shared volume
A container dies mid-clone holding the lock
findings.suggested_fix: Clone into a sibling temp dir (e.g. "$DIR.provisioning.$$") and only `mv` it onto $DIR once the clone (and ensure) succeed; the rename is atomic on the same filesystem, so concurrent containers either see the old store or the fully-provisioned new one, never a cleared dir mid-clone.

The fix newly triggers clear+reclone on every currently-poisoned volume at first deploy, re-creating the same long-clone-vs-readiness race the plan blames for the original poisoning.
ABSENCE: no acceptance criterion or rollout note states how the first deploy against poisoned volumes reaches a healthy resolvable HEAD without being rolled back mid-clone.

The plan specifies backgrounding + a lock for steady state but does not state how the first rollout of this fix — where every poisoned volume must clear 1.5G and re-clone — survives the readiness window / blue-green rollback that repeatedly killed mid-clone containers.
